\title{Periodicity, Not Length: Locating the Repetition-Counting\\
       Failure in Neural Text-to-Speech}

\twoauthors
  {Ivan Viakhirev$^{1}$, Kirill Borodin$^{2,3}$, Grach Mkrtchian$^{2}$}
  {$^{1}$ITMO University, Russia \\
   $^{2}$lab260, Moscow Technical University of Communications and Informatics, Russia \\
   $^{3}$BitmanagerAI, UAE}
  {}{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Text-to-speech models loop, truncate and lose count on text that repeats a
phrase many times. We isolate what drives it with a parametric repetition
ladder: \NStimuli{} stimuli in which a target word recurs $k$ times, each paired
with a \emph{length-matched control} of the same carrier and word count whose
repeated token is replaced by distinct fillers. Across \NModels{} checkpoints
from \NFamilies{} architectures, models render repeated text exactly in
\ExactRep{}\% of generations against \ExactCtl{}\% for their controls at
$k\ge6$: a gap of \FamExact{} points $[\FamExactLo{},\FamExactHi{}]$ by
architecture family ($n{=}\FamExactN{}$), favouring the control in all
\CkExactN{} checkpoints, and \FullLadderGap{} points over the whole ladder from
$k{=}1$. The limit tracks \emph{periodicity, not length}. It survives greedy decoding, an
order-of-magnitude repetition-penalty sweep, checkpoints that pass no penalty at
all, never-cycled controls, and every exclusion rule switched off
(\ExSensAll{} points). Measuring it needs care: the obvious judge, Whisper, is
autoregressive and biased \emph{against} the phenomenon, scoring
\WhisperValPer{} of the true count on periodic ground truth where a CTC
recogniser scores \CtcValPer{}. Nor is the failure peculiar to autoregressive
decoding --- of two non-autoregressive baselines one is immune and one is not.
We also state and machine-check in Lean~4 a conditional bound: if the
per-repetition state map contracts with factor $q<1$, no Lipschitz readout can
separate counts past a computable horizon. We report it as a motivating
conjecture and not an explanation: two attempts to measure $q$ failed, and the
companion dilution lemma's one directional prediction came out sign-reversed.
The empirical result stands independently of it.
\end{abstract}

\begin{keywords}
speech synthesis, hallucination, probing, autoregressive models,
formal verification
\end{keywords}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Ask an autoregressive text-to-speech (TTS) model to say \emph{six hundred
sixty-six thousand six hundred sixty-six}, or to repeat a word a dozen times, and
it will frequently get the count wrong: it stops early, runs on, or locks into a
loop. The behaviour is documented as a stability
problem~\cite{song2024ellav,wang2023valle} and usually attributed to
exposure bias or to the absence of a monotonic alignment constraint, with fixes
proposed at the level of attention supervision or decoding
rules~\cite{xin2024ralle,du2024cosyvoice2} --- the speech analogue of neural text
degeneration~\cite{holtzman2020curious,welleck2020neural}.

Reports of this behaviour confound two things, because repeating a phrase $k$
times makes the text both \emph{longer} and \emph{periodic}. If long inputs are
simply harder --- through attention span, exposure bias or a duration budget ---
then nothing about repetition needs explaining. The manipulation here separates
them by construction: every repeated item is paired with a
\emph{length-matched control} of the same carrier and the same word count, in
which the $k$ copies of one word become $k$ non-adjacent distinct ones. A
length account predicts the two curves coincide. They do not, and that contrast
is the paper's sharpest result.

Measuring it is its own problem, because the natural instrument shares the
failure it is meant to detect: a judge biased in the direction of the effect can
manufacture it. That constrains the design rather than decorating it, and
Section~\ref{sec:method} treats it as a result in its own right.

We contribute, in order of what the evidence supports: a controlled
manipulation that isolates periodicity from length across \NModels{}
checkpoints and two non-autoregressive baselines, on which the deficit tracks
periodicity and survives the field's standard mitigations; a judge methodology
for repetitive speech, the obvious judge shown to be disqualified; and an
account of \emph{where} the failure sits, separating what the decoder
represents from what its output policy uses. A conditional impossibility result,
machine-checked in Lean~4, motivated the study; we report it as a conjecture
whose premise we could not measure and whose one directional prediction our data
contradict. The work is a companion to a spectral study of hallucination in
encoder--decoder ASR~\cite{viakhirev2026dispersion}.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\noindent\textbf{Stimuli.}
A parametric repetition ladder of \NStimuli{} items: carrier sentences with a
target word repeated $k \in \{1,2,3,4,6,8,12,16,24,32\}$ times, plus repeated
sentences, tongue twisters and English number phrases with intrinsic digit-word
repetition. Every word- and sentence-repetition item at $k\ge2$ has a
\emph{length-matched control}: same carrier and word count, the repeated token
replaced by fillers from a per-template pool of eight, cycled above $k\!=\!8$
(S10).

\noindent\textbf{Models.}
The panel is \NModels{} checkpoints but only \NFamilies{} designs, scale
variants making up the difference: Llasa at 1B/3B/8B (Llama backbones over X-codec2
tokens~\cite{ye2025llasa}) and Qwen3-TTS at 0.6B/1.7B are within-architecture
ladders, plus XTTS-v2~\cite{casanova2024xtts}. VITS~\cite{kim2021vits} and
F5-TTS~\cite{chen2024f5tts} run as non-autoregressive baselines, XTTS-v2 and
Qwen3-TTS-0.6B at altered repetition penalty as ablations; neither group is
pooled into the panel. Every arm renders every item at \NSeeds{} seeds.

\noindent\textbf{Behavioural measurement, and why the obvious judge is wrong.}
The natural instrument, Whisper large-v3~\cite{radford2023whisper}, is
demonstrably the wrong one: its decoder is autoregressive with a language-model
prior, so it is subject to the very dynamics under study. Audited against
concatenative audio with known ground truth its counted/true ratio falls to
$0.27$--$0.65$ over $k\ge4$ and to \WhisperValPer{} at the top of the ladder,
while \emph{same-voice distinct-word} sequences of identical length score
$1.00$: a bias specific to periodicity, pointing the way of the effect we want
to measure. We score instead with a CTC recogniser
(\texttt{wav2vec2-large-960h-lv60-self}, greedy best-path, no language model),
put through the same audit --- ratio \CtcValPer{} on the same ground truth.
Worse in absolute WER, right for this purpose. Both transcript sets are
released.

$\hat c$ is obtained by matching the target unit against the transcript's word
sequence, counting non-overlapping occurrences in order and skipping
unrecognised ones rather than stopping at the first miss, which would void
credit for every later filler in a control. The reported quantity is the
\emph{relative count error} $(\hat c - k)/k$; exact-match scores $30$-of-$32$
and $3$-of-$32$ alike. Of \MainNGen{} panel generations we exclude
\MainExclTmpl{} in one template whose fillers the judge never transcribes,
\MainExclCap{} stopped by our token budget rather than by the model, and
\MainExclDegen{} degenerate, leaving \MainKept{}; S10 gives per-condition rates.

\noindent\textbf{State measurement.}
For each instrumented generation we record per-step hidden states at probe
layers and head-averaged attention onto the text span. \emph{Effective rank} is the
exponentiated Shannon entropy of the trajectory's normalised singular-value
spectrum; the count probe is ridge regression ($\alpha{=}1$ throughout) on
mean-pooled states, the layer chosen by leave-one-template-out $R^2$ (S6).

\noindent\textbf{Code, data, settings.}
Lean development, stimuli, code, per-item tables, the full supplement and both
transcript sets are public at tag \texttt{v1.1-icassp} of
\url{https://github.com/lab260ru/icassp_antispoofing} (name predates this
study). \texttt{build.sh} regenerates every number here from pinned revisions
(S19), and a stratified \SampleN{}-clip sample spanning every model, $k$ band
and outcome ships with each clip's transcript and scoring decision, so a
judgement can be checked by ear. Audio and activations regenerate from the
released seeds. Sampling uses shipped defaults (XTTS-v2
$T{=}0.75$/$0.85$/$50$/penalty $5.0$; Llasa $T{=}0.8$, top-$p$ $1.0$; Qwen3-TTS
$T{=}0.9$/$1.0$/$50$/$1.05$), making Qwen3-TTS the \emph{most} stochastic
family, so its larger checkpoint's null is not an artifact of conservative
decoding. The penalty is the one parameter we vary.

\section{A Candidate Mechanism, and the Evidence Against It}
\label{sec:theory}

One mechanism for a periodicity-specific limit can be stated exactly, so we
state it and then report that our own tests of it failed. Softmax attention over
$k$ repeated spans whose logits differ by at most $\delta$ gives each weight in
$[e^{-\delta}/k,e^{\delta}/k]$, so the profile flattens (Lemma~1). A decoder
that cannot tell the spans apart meets the same conditioning at every
\emph{repetition boundary}, making the map $F$ between consecutive boundary
states autonomous; if $F$ is a $q$-contraction with orbit scale $C$, boundary
states converge geometrically and no $L$-Lipschitz readout --- the stop head
included --- separates counts with margin $\mu$ beyond
$N^\ast=\log(\mu/2LC)/\log q$ (Theorem~1). Both are machine-checked in Lean~4
over \texttt{mathlib}, free of \texttt{sorry} and with an axiom audit;
statements, proofs, and a clause-by-clause correspondence to their informal
versions are in S1--S2.

\emph{We could not measure the premise, and the lemma's one directional
prediction came out backwards.} Two independent estimators of $q$ failed: one
needs a monotone attention read-head these decoders lack --- the flatter the
profile, the worse any attention-based localiser, so Lemma~1 undercuts it
structurally --- and a finite-difference probe found no repeated-versus-control
difference ($7/18$ pairs, $p=0.12$) while failing its own linearity control
(S5). Lemma~1's premise itself holds only approximately
($\delta\le\DeltaMax{}$ nats). And its dose-response prediction is not merely
untested but \emph{disconfirmed}: within a $(\text{model},k)$ cell, flatter
attention goes with \emph{better} counting ($r=\DilR{}$
$[\DilRLo{},\DilRHi{}]$; S12), the opposite of what dilution-driven collapse
requires. We report the bound because it is what motivated the study, not
because the data support it; nothing in Section~\ref{sec:results} rests on it.
